title: Thesis
text:
This page collects material related to my Master’s thesis.
The thesis was written in Italian; an English version will be available soon.





Original title: Metodi numerici proiettivi con componente probabilistica per equazioni matriciali lineari
Degree: Master’s Degree in Mathematics
Institution: Alma Mater Studiorum — Università di Bologna
Academic year: 2023–2024
Advisor: Prof. Valeria Simoncini
Area: Numerical Analysis



This thesis concerns the efficient numerical solution of large-scale linear matrix equations. In this context, Krylov subspace methods play a central role, since they exploit the structure and sparsity of the matrices involved and construct low-rank approximations to the solution.
A key computational bottleneck in Krylov methods is the orthogonalization of the basis, whose cost increases with the number of iterations. Truncated Krylov methods reduce this cost by limiting the dimension of the projection space, but they may suffer from delayed convergence or stagnation, especially for more complex matrix equations.
The thesis investigates the use of randomized sketching techniques to overcome these limitations. Sketching projects the original data onto a lower-dimensional random space while preserving the essential features of the problem. The main goal of the work is to combine sketching and truncation in order to reduce the computational cost of projection methods while maintaining good convergence properties.
The study focuses on linear matrix equations more general than the Sylvester equation, including problems of the form
\[
A_1 X B_1^T + A_2 X B_2^T + \cdots + A_m X B_m^T = C_1 C_2^T
\]
where the coefficient matrices are sparse, symmetric and positive definite. A simpler model problem of the form
\[
AX + XA^T + MXM^T = CC^T
\]
is also analyzed. The thesis develops and tests algorithms based on embedding subspaces and sketching, with numerical experiments comparing the proposed approach with existing methods.

title: Matrix Nearness Problems: When a Matrix Is Almost Right
text:
Matrices appear naturally in many areas of applied mathematics and scientific computing. They are used to represent data, transformations, interactions between variables, discretized differential operators, and many other objects.
Very often, a matrix is expected to satisfy some structural property. A covariance matrix should be positive semidefinite. A correlation matrix should be symmetric, positive semidefinite, and have diagonal entries equal to one. A matrix representing an orthogonal transformation should remain orthogonal.
In practice, however, matrices are frequently obtained from data, measurements, simulations, or finite-precision computations. Because of noise, missing information, or rounding errors, the matrix we obtain may be close to having the desired property, but not quite.
This leads to a natural question:

If a matrix almost satisfies a desired property, can we replace it by the nearest matrix that does?

This is the basic idea behind matrix nearness problems.



✕


Noisy or imperfect data


A matrix is estimated or computed, but it does not satisfy the required property.



→



↦


Matrix nearness problem


Find the closest matrix satisfying the desired structure.



→



✓


Valid structured matrix


The corrected matrix is usable while remaining close to the original one.



Figure 1. Matrix nearness problems provide a systematic way to correct an imperfect matrix while changing it as little as possible.


Consider the matrix
\[
A=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0.9 \\
0.9 & -0.1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This matrix is symmetric, which is often a desirable property. However, it is not positive semidefinite because one of its eigenvalues is negative.
If \(A\) is intended to represent a covariance matrix, then this creates a problem: covariance matrices must be positive semidefinite. In other words, the matrix is very close to being admissible, but it fails to satisfy an essential requirement.
Rather than discarding the data and starting over, we may ask:

What is the closest positive semidefinite matrix to \(A\)?

This is a typical matrix nearness problem.
The goal is not to find an arbitrary positive semidefinite matrix, but rather to make the smallest possible modification to the original matrix while restoring the desired property.
Even in this simple example, a seemingly straightforward question naturally leads to ideas from matrix analysis, optimization, and spectral theory.



A matrix nearness problem can often be written in the form
\[
\min_{X \in \mathcal{S}} \|A-X\|,
\]
where \(A\) is the given matrix, \(\mathcal{S}\) is a set of matrices satisfying a certain property, and \(\|\cdot\|\) is a chosen matrix norm.
The set \(\mathcal{S}\) may consist, for example, of

positive semidefinite matrices;
correlation matrices;
covariance matrices;
orthogonal matrices;
low-rank matrices;
stable matrices;
matrices with prescribed sparsity or structure.

Different choices of \(\mathcal{S}\) lead to different mathematical and computational problems.



Matrix nearness problems are not only abstract approximation problems. They appear naturally whenever structure matters.


Covariance and correlation matrices are central in statistics and data science. However, matrices estimated from data may fail to be positive semidefinite because of noise, incomplete observations, or numerical errors.
In such cases, one may want to replace the estimated matrix by the nearest valid covariance or correlation matrix.



A particularly important example is the nearest correlation matrix problem.
In finance, large correlation matrices are used in portfolio optimization, risk management, and derivative pricing. Empirical correlation matrices may fail to be valid correlation matrices, especially when data are incomplete or inconsistent.
Nicholas Higham’s 2002 paper on the nearest correlation matrix problem is one of the standard references in this direction.



Many numerical algorithms are designed around matrices with special structure. For example, symmetry, orthogonality, and positive definiteness are often essential for stability and efficiency.
During a computation, these properties may be slightly lost. A matrix nearness approach gives a systematic way to restore them.



In some applications, it is important to know how far a matrix is from having an undesirable property. For example, one may ask how far a stable matrix is from becoming unstable.
This point of view connects matrix nearness problems with eigenvalue optimization and spectral analysis.




Although the basic idea is easy to state, matrix nearness problems can be mathematically subtle.
Some natural questions are:

Does a nearest matrix always exist?
Is it unique?
Can it be characterized explicitly?
Can it be computed efficiently?
How does the answer depend on the chosen norm?
What happens when the matrix is very large or has additional structure?

These questions connect matrix nearness problems with numerical linear algebra, optimization, matrix analysis, and spectral theory.
In modern applications, the computational aspect is especially important. A theoretically elegant solution may be too expensive for large matrices, so efficient algorithms become essential.



Matrix nearness problems provide a useful framework for dealing with matrices that are almost, but not exactly, structurally correct.
The central idea is simple: given a matrix that fails to satisfy a desired property, find the closest matrix that does. This idea appears in many areas, from statistics and finance to control theory and scientific computing.
In future notes, I will discuss some specific examples in more detail, starting with the nearest correlation matrix problem.



[1] N. J. Higham, Matrix Nearness Problems and Applications, in Applications of Matrix Theory, Oxford University Press, 1989.
[2] N. J. Higham, Computing the Nearest Correlation Matrix—A Problem from Finance, IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis, 22(3), pp. 329–343, 2002.
[3] N. Guglielmi and C. Lubich, Matrix Nearness Problems and Eigenvalue Optimization, arXiv:2503.14750, 2025.
